summary: Defines a notation for describing protocol layers in a protocol encapsulation, for encoding INDEX values for the protocolDirTable in the RMON-2 MIB. It is on the standards track at the draft standard level.

eli5.summary: A short code spells out the stack of wrappers a packet is in. This explains how to write those codes for a network monitoring tool.

subtitle: The naming scheme that lets an RMON probe say exactly which stack of protocol wrappers it is counting.

tldr.problem: The RMON-2 protocol directory has to identify each protocol encapsulation, such as SNMP over UDP over IP over Ethernet, with one globally agreed index value.
tldr.mechanism: Each layer is encoded as a 4-octet layer-identifier, and the identifiers are concatenated left to right starting with a base layer. A parallel string holds one parameter octet per layer, and a small macro notation describes each protocol.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2895 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2074 and carries the normative rules and base-layer identifiers. The example macros moved to RFC 2896, and RFC 2895 has been updated by RFC 3395.

today: RFC 2895 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2074, and it has been updated by RFC 3395. The collection of protocol identifier macros it split off is in RFC 2896.

sections.title: What This Document Does
sections.content:
The RMON-2 MIB (RFC 2021) uses hierarchically formatted OCTET STRINGs to globally identify individual protocol encapsulations in its protocolDirTable. RFC 2895 contains the algorithms and the authoritative set of base layer protocol identifier macros for building the INDEX values of that table. It does not specify a MIB module itself.

It replaces the first half of RFC 2074. That first RMON Protocol Identifiers document was split in two: this standards-track reference, and an Informational document, RFC 2896, which holds the non-normative collection of protocol identifier macros. The split lets the list of macros change without republishing MIB objects or encoding rules.

The document is intentionally separate from the RMON-2 MIB objects so it can be updated on its own. It does not discuss auto-discovery of the protocolDirTable, which the RMON standard does not define; an agent SHOULD populate the directory with the interesting protocols its applications depend on.
sections.eli5: Network monitors need a common way to name each kind of wrapped-up packet. This is the rulebook for the names, and the long list of examples lives in a different book.

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content:
A layer-identifier is an octet string fragment for one encapsulation layer or sub-layer, always exactly four octets in network byte order. A protocol-identifier string is made of one or more layer-identifiers read left to right: the left-most is a base layer, and each one to its right is a child. In RMON-2 this string is the protocolDirID object.

A parent protocol encapsulates a child protocol; IP is the parent of UDP, and UDP is a child of IP. Base layers cannot have parents. Together, the encapsulations form an inverted protocol encapsulation tree, whose roots are the base encapsulations.

A protocol-parameters string (protocolDirParameters) holds one single-octet bit-mask for each layer-identifier. A protocol-identifier macro, or PI macro, is a textual construct that names a protocol, says how it is encoded, how its children are identified and which parameters are allowed. The word macro is historical: PI macros are not real macros.

A protocol-variant-identifier macro is a special PI macro for protocols that cannot be identified from their traffic, used for IANA-assigned protocols. A pseudo-protocol is a convention used only within this document to encode identifier strings.
sections.eli5: Think of a set of nesting dolls. Each doll gets a short tag, and the line of tags from the biggest doll inward names exactly which doll you mean.

sections.title: Protocol Identifier Encoding
sections.content:
The protocolDirTable is indexed by two OCTET STRINGs: protocolDirID and protocolDirParameters. Each is converted to an OBJECT IDENTIFIER fragment using the encoding rules in section 7.7 of RFC 1902, and the two fragments are concatenated. Each string is preceded by a length sub-component.

The first string is made of N layer-identifiers of 4 octets each, so it is 4 times N octets long. The second string has N octets, one parameter octet per layer. In the RFC's example, N equals 4, so the first length sub-component is 16 and the second is 4. Each layer-identifier is a 32-bit value written as four sub-components in network byte order. A layer that cannot fit in 32 bits has to be defined as an ianaAssigned protocol.

When an index is evaluated, the protocolDirID length MUST be evenly divisible by four, and the parameters string MUST be exactly one quarter of that length. Parsing begins with the base layer identifier, which MUST be present. Layers MUST NOT be skipped, so identifiers such as SNMP over IP, or TCP over ether2, cannot exist.

A label may map to more than one value. For example, ip maps to 5 distinct values, one for each supported encapsulation. These macros are expanded at implementation time, not at run time.
sections.eli5: Every wrapper gets a four-number tag. Line the tags up from the outside in, and you have the full name of the packet. A second short list says which extra tricks the monitor should do for each wrapper.

sections.title: The Protocol Identifier Macro
sections.content:
PI macros are written in a small language with the keywords PROTOCOL-IDENTIFIER, VARIANT-OF, PARAMETERS, ATTRIBUTES, DESCRIPTION, CHILDREN, ADDRESS-FORMAT, DECODING and REFERENCE. The RFC specifies its grammar in extended BNF.

A protocol name is one to 64 characters from letters, digits, dash, underbar, asterisk and plus. It SHOULD match the most well-known name for the protocol. Characters not allowed in a name MUST be changed to a dash, so z39.50 becomes z39-50.

The PARAMETERS, ATTRIBUTES and DESCRIPTION clauses MUST be present in every macro, though the first two may be empty. CHILDREN MUST be present when the hasChildren(0) bit is set, and ADDRESS-FORMAT MUST be present when addressRecognitionCapable(1) is set. DECODING is optional, and REFERENCE is optional but SHOULD be given if an authoritative document exists.

The VARIANT-OF clause is present only for IANA-assigned protocols. It names the closest documented protocol, the reference protocol, and the variant macro then carries empty parameter and attribute lists.
sections.eli5: Each protocol gets a small fact sheet with set boxes: its name, what it is, what can sit inside it, and where to read more.

sections.title: Parameters and Attributes
sections.content:
The protocolDirParameters octet lets a manager switch expensive probe resources on or off for each layer. An agent may support a parameter all the time, not at all, or depending on its current load. Bit 0 is the high-order bit of the octet, and unused bits are set to zero. Two bit positions are reserved by convention and MUST NOT be used for other purposes.

countsFragments(0) says the probe correctly attributes all fragmented packets of the protocol, even if individual frames cannot be identified as carrying it. It may be set only for a protocol that supports fragmentation and reassembly; TCP is not eligible. tracksSessions(1) says frames in remapped sessions, such as TFTP downloads that move from a well-known port to a dynamic one, are counted correctly, which requires the probe to keep some state.

The ATTRIBUTES clause fills in protocolDirType. hasChildren(0) says children of the protocol may be defined, and addressRecognitionCapable(1) says the protocol can be used to generate host and matrix table entries.
sections.eli5: Some wrappers need the monitor to work harder, like remembering where a conversation moved to. A switch per wrapper lets the manager turn that extra effort on or off.

sections.title: Base Layers and Wildcards
sections.content:
The first layer, the base identifier, is four octets: a special function code f, two operands op1 and op2, and the base layer enumeration value m. Function 0 means none, with both operands zero. Function 1, the wildcard, lets one entry aggregate counters across many base layer encapsulations of the same network layer protocol. Its operands MUST be zero, and it should be defined using the lowest base layer value that permits the encapsulation.

Only 255 base layer encapsulations are supported by design, and five are defined: ether2, llc, snap, vsnap and ianaAssigned. Children of ether2 are chosen by the Ethernet-II type field, and the RFC notes that only type values greater than 1500 decimal indicate Ethernet-II frames. Children of llc are chosen by the SAP value, with the SSAP matched first. Children of snap use the Ethernet-II type value, and vsnap covers SNAP packets whose OUI is not zero.

The ianaAssigned base layer is for protocols that cannot be identified by examining traffic. In the IANA Considerations, only one protocol is defined under it, ipxOverRaw8023.

An encapsulation layer such as IEEE 802.1Q VLAN tagging may sit between the base layer and the network layer. The RFC defines a PI macro, 802-1Q, that supports most but not all of its features. For instance, it does not expose the Token Ring encapsulation bit in the TCI field.
sections.eli5: Every packet starts in one of five kinds of outer envelope. The first tag says which envelope, and one special tag says to count the same contents no matter which envelope.

sections.title: Relationship to ATM and Other MIBs
sections.content:
The RMON PI document has no explicit macros for ATM encapsulations such as RFC 1483 or LAN Emulation (LANE). Instead, a probe must fit the ATM encapsulation to one of the base layers llc, snap or vsnap. A manager can recover some omitted details from the ifType of the data source, such as aal5(49) for RFC 1483 and aflane8023(59) or aflane8025(60) for LANE. These data sources need the ifStackTable from the Interfaces MIB.

For octet counters in RMON-2 host and matrix tables, a probe must use the AAL-5 frame size, not the AAL-5 payload size or the encapsulated MAC frame size.

The RFC says this document is not relevant to any MIB other than the RMON protocolDirTable. Changes from RFC 2074 are listed in Appendix A, including a clarification that the countsFragments bit may be set in more than one parameter octet of an index.
sections.eli5: ATM wraps data in its own special way. The monitor squeezes it into the closest of the five standard envelopes and counts it that way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it discusses the syntax and semantics of textual descriptions of networking protocols, not the definition of any networking behavior. As a result, it says no security considerations are raised by this memo.
sections.eli5: This rulebook only explains how to write names down, so it does not add any new security worries of its own.

fields.desc: Special function code: 0 for none, 1 for wildcard.

viz.caption: TWO EXAMPLE protocolDirTable INDEX VALUES, COPIED FROM THE RFC

data.title: Encoded index examples
data.code:
-- HTTP; fragments counted from IP and above
ether2.ip.tcp.www-http =
   16.0.0.0.1.0.0.8.0.0.0.0.6.0.0.0.80.4.0.1.0.0

-- SNMP over UDP/IP over SNAP
snap.ip.udp.snmp =
   16.0.0.0.3.0.0.8.0.0.0.0.17.0.0.0.161.4.0.0.0.0
